On the readthrough to October core PCE both BofA and Goldman significantly raised their expectations: 

Bank of America said the CPI data “topped our expectations, driven in part by broad-based strength in goods inflation. This could be evidence of energy and AI related input cost pass through.” It is now tracking October core PCE at 0.32% month over month, up from its initial 0.23% estimate, which it said “would lift the y/y rate to 3.3% from 3.1%, which is a clearly hawkish development.” For headline PCE, it is tracking 0.34% and 3.9% from a year earlier.

“Our core PCE tracking estimate would meet Governor Waller’s threshold for a 50bp hike in December based on his remarks from this morning,” Bank of America said. “That helps explain the move in market pricing. We still think the Fed goes 25bp for now, but the door to a larger hike at its next meeting has opened further after today’s data.”

Goldman Sachs now estimates that core PCE rose 0.35% in October, up from its 0.23% expectation before the CPI release, “corresponding to a year-over-year rate of +3.30%,” with headline PCE up 0.36%, or 3.87% from a year earlier.

 It said the core CPI surprise “was driven by firmer-than-expected readings in a broad set of categories,” with owners’ equivalent rent “firm for the second consecutive month” and “concentrated in the Midwest,” and motor vehicle insurance prices rebounding “after running softer this year.” Medical services rose “despite a decline in health insurance prices following the BLS’ incorporation of updated source data on insurance premiums.”

Logan's speech is now posted (link at the bottom - h/t @Fedwatchenjoyer), and a few other points stand out. 

She said this morning’s CPI “was higher than expected” and that “I am concerned that PCE inflation could rise when we receive those data for October in a couple of weeks.” 

She like Waller, though, isn't calling for a dramatic hiking cycle: “I currently estimate that the fed funds target range is at least 50 basis points—half a percentage point—below the level that would create some modest restriction and begin to bring the inflation trend back to target.” 

But she notes the real fed funds rate is just 78 basis points (the 3.88% fed funds rate less the roughly 3.1% inflation that households, businesses and markets expect), a quarter point below the lowest of eight model estimates of neutral, so “accommodative monetary policy is adding to inflationary pressures.”

And like the other Fed speakers since Thursday, she isn't moved by the market declines. Financial conditions “are currently providing a tailwind,” with credit spreads still “compressed by historical standards,” and the rise in 10-year yields is “more a message that investors believe monetary policy has work to do than an independent headwind for activity.”

On October’s skip, she said the volatile markets argued for moving “more gradually,” but “Skipping one meeting does not change the monetary policy destination,” and “the precise timing of each rate increase has little effect on the longer-term rates most borrowers pay.” After two more hikes, “it would make sense in my view to pause and examine economic and financial developments.”

And like Goolsbee yesterday, she pointed to services which came in elevated in October. “Prices for non-housing, non-transportation core services rose 3.2% over the 12 months ended in September,” eight tenths of a point above the pace consistent with the Fed’s target, and those prices “aren’t particularly sensitive to tariffs, conflict in the Middle East or surging demand for computer chips.” 

But she downplayed her own bank’s inflation gauge. The Dallas Fed’s trimmed mean PCE was lower, at 2.3% over the 12 months through September, but she said her staff’s research finds “a change in the mix of price increases and decreases is causing the trimmed mean to drop too many increases right now,” which “likely makes the trimmed mean lower than the true inflation trend.”

tweets.text:
But wait... there's more!

In January, SoftBank's SB Energy, the developer building the massive Ohio and Texas data center campuses, granted warrants to OpenAI as a "lease incentive" for signing a data center lease in Milam County, Texas. That's right: the landlord paid the tenant, in equity, to rent the building. Some of those warrants were forfeited in August when OpenAI signed the 20-year Ohio lease, but ¥542 billion ($3.4 billion) of them still sit on SoftBank's balance sheet as a derivative liability.

And here is the punchline: because the warrants get more valuable as SB Energy does, every time the data center business is marked higher, SoftBank books a loss, ¥204 billion in the first half, plus another ¥136 billion of share-based compensation for the unit's staff for the same reason. A business whose success shows up as a loss is a neat trick even by AI-bubble standards.

But the circularity doesn't end there:

Nvidia, the exclusive chip supplier for the Ohio campus, has wired $1.5 billion to SB Energy under a share issuance agreement and is providing credit support for OpenAI on the first 4.25 gigawatts. So the chip vendor (NVDA) funds the landlord (Softbank) and backstops the tenant (OpenAI), who then buys the chips (NVDA).

SoftBank Corp, the listed Japanese telecom arm, sold its SB Energy stake to Vision Fund 2 and booked an ¥80 billion gain. One SoftBank pocket selling to another (for a "profit"): the gain vanishes on consolidation, but it looks great at the telco, and a whole bunch of clueless Japanese momentum-chasers buy something that moves higher.

The Vision Funds, meanwhile, marked down their stakes in SoftBank's own subsidiaries, mainly SB7 (the turbine buyer) and PayPay, by ¥364 billion. That one vanishes on consolidation too.

And SB Energy's IPO, which was supposed to crystallize a $50 billion-plus valuation, has been frozen since September due to regulatory issues well before the midterms.

Gather round folks, because just when you thought Masa Son would not catalyze the bursting of the next bubble... well, read for yourselves

SoftBank bought 87 million Intel shares for $2 billion last year. By the end of March the stake was worth $3.8 billion, and by the end of September $10.5 billion, good for a ¥1.06 trillion gain in the first half. 

Instead of selling, in August SoftBank did something much more, well, SoftBank: it raised $7.35 billion through prepaid forward contracts on its entire Intel stake, structured as collars with a floor and a cap. In English, it borrowed more than three times what it paid for the stock, pledged every share, and sold away the upside above the cap to pay for the downside protection.

What happened next? Intel shares kept climbing after the ink dried, which means the capped contracts moved against SoftBank, to the tune of a ¥322 billion ($2 billion) derivative loss in less than two months. And because Intel still finished the September quarter below where it started, SoftBank also booked a ¥270 billion valuation loss on the shares themselves.

So in a single quarter Masa managed to lose money on the stock and on the hedge. That takes sheer talent.

The fine print is even better: of the ¥1.65 trillion of Intel shares pledged, the banks have "rights of use" over ¥1.1 trillion, meaning they are free to lend out or otherwise use SoftBank's collateral.

Some important things to understand about market structure:
-fundamentally nothing has changed since 10/10 re: alts and arguably has gotten worse
-as such, liquid funds can’t size as big on alt allocations. This was the main structural bid on “quality alts” in the past. Most people are just trading momentum/trend
-Capital / margin is more spread out because of the growth of cross-marginable stock / RWA perps. Fiat stables haven’t grown their market cap in some time now
-leakage: Hacks, exchange fees, launchpads, grifters. Same as before but recent uptick in hacks due to AI cyber capabilities 
-so who has money? (1) Basis/systematic traders who got favorably ADL’d on 10/10 ie not a source of bid on market beta (2) HYPE airdrop recipients/holders, who are mostly losing traders / momentum types (3) hackers who sell coins -> fiat

These aspects all contribute to crypto trading like absolute garbage outside of some short periods where people are forced to chase aggressively trending coins

On the Nvidia situation:

Nvidia, $NVDA, is now down another -7% today and -12% since the Jensen Huang affair situation began.

At this point, the market is pricing in two major potential headwinds.

First, the growing possibility that Jensen Huang will be removed as CEO.

Second, possibility that sensitive Nvidia technology or information was compromised.

Are these scenarios possible? Sure, but we believe both remain unlikely, with less than a 20% probability.

Nvidia's stock is now down -32% in just 24 trading days, erasing -$1.8 trillion in market cap, with over one-third of these losses coinciding with the Jensen Huang controversy.

We believe Huang remains an integral part of Nvidia's future and the broader AI Revolution, and this week's events will not derail the broader thesis.

As the dust settles and uncertainty begins to fade, we expect bargain hunters to step in.

The fundamental AI investment thesis remains intact.

tweets.text: The stock market has been walked down for over a month, in the case of small caps, over 2 months. As someone who has been shorting bounces during that time period, I now think that is a dangerous reflex here. We had a climactic selling event last week, a strong bounce and are now approaching the first test of whether or not the trend of the previous weeks continues. The event calendar and ongoing risks look much different over the next four weeks than they did going into the previous four weeks. This move is getting long in the tooth and I think it's more likely than not that Waller's speech + today's CPI has provided an attractive opportunity to flip from a short to a long risk bias into next week's Anthropic IPO and possibly longer, TBD. This is not an all clear of the structural problems that exist, but a local call that the path to the final destination will not be easy nor in a straight line.

On the plus side, he finally got the data piece right, but he has ramped up the hawkish tone into what is likely to be the very pico top of inflation (cyclically). On a multi-week to multi-month time horizon, this is a fade.

"ETH is dead."

I've heard this a gazillion times already.

Still, I think people underestimate how valuable it is to have a network that nobody can easily control or shut down.

@VitalikButerin makes a fair point here. Too many people treat the ETH burn like a scoreboard for its value.

Sure, burning fees helps, but Ethereum's biggest strengths have always been its:

→ Decentralization
→ Security
→ Resistance to outside control

And that's the challenge for Fusaka and Glamsterdam - helping Ethereum handle more transactions without giving a handful of players more control over the network.

ETH's long-term value depends far more on these qualities than on how much supply gets burned.

tweets.text:
Here's my analogy for Elysium:

Imagine someone is exploring a desert in the middle of California.

They think "Man, California is a really popular state and a lot of people live in some of the big cities... imagine if this desert had water. Well, I'm sure people would move out here! And if they wanted to move out here, there would definitely need to be some roads... so I'll build the roads to the desert just in case there's ever water because then people would definitely want to build businesses... why? Because the desert is in California! So there'd obviously be a need for it."

So that person then creates a sales deck for a new community smack dab in the middle of the desert. They pitch the idea that there's enough growth elsewhere in the state that most likely they'll probably eventually find water, and it makes sense to a lot of people... because people in California like California.

And the cool part? The land in the new community is still so dang cheap! And the rest of the state is so expensive that when the people come out there, it's probably gonna boom.

So they buy the cheap land, and start building businesses because there were roads to get there.

And while the businesses are being built the community IS booming.

The people that bought the land struck gold!

Then slowly but surely, the building stops... and the people that were building have no reason to be there anymore because their job is finished... and then, nobody is left in the community.

Why?

Because they built it before they ever found the water.

They built it in anticipation that one day they might.

And that was enough for a bit... but at the end of the day, they're still in a desert and nobody is going to go out there unless there's an actual need to do it.

So, the roads still exist.

The empty buildings still exist.

But they slowly decay until people forget they ever did.

3/ concordium:native Utility

Concordium offers sponsored transactions, meaning the user never touches CCD, but the sponsor still pays the fee in concordium:native.

tweets.text:
I wouldn't characterize the state of enterprise AI adoption this way. Broadly, I would say there are two variables in measuring the ROI of AI in an organization: 
1. The task you are automating or augmenting 
2. Does this business have any fucking idea why they are successful? 

#1 The task. 
Let's take a very simple example. Closing out a support ticket from a customer. Most companies know how much this costs by channel - say, $40 to pick up the phone, $15 to answer it by email, $5 by chat. This is calculating using things like the agent salaries, the headcount that supports them, the technology they use, the facilities, and any travel and training expenses

Now imagine you can use AI to *successfully* answer a question and the AI company you use charges you 70 cents for that. OK, you really clearly know the ROI of AI in this specific, bounded, use case.

Consider other tasks. The velocity with which you ship new products. A bit fuzzier but not a crazy task to determine whether 1) Developer productivity has increased 2) Whether that is bending the slope of your revenue curve upward.

Farther out on the curve. Being able to now generate 21 different versions of a marketing campaign's creative using your brand design assets. Making 40% of analytics requests self-service instead of being stuck in a queue for humans to answer. Quite a bit messier to measure direct ROI.

#2 Does the company have it's shit together? 

Do they know what is actually driving the business forward? I think that the answer for many businesses is actually, No. Do they reliably know who their top performers are? Do they know the actual 2-3 inputs that drive revenue growth? Not only do they know them but can they accelerate them? If you asked 10 people at the company what "the most important thing" was for the business, would they give the same answer? Again, I think the answer is mostly No. 

If you do not deeply understand your business, what is driving it, and who is driving it, it is quite hard to know whether AI is helping you. 
----------
TL;DR. For some tasks it is quite easy to measure the ROI. For others, less so. For some businesses who have their shit together, it is quite easy to measure the ROI. For others, less so.

🔥No official U.S. CPI YoY number today — but we can still estimate it.

Because of the 2025 government shutdown, BLS never collected October 2025 CPI data, leaving it unable to calculate the usual year-over-year comparison for today’s release.

We backfilled the missing October 2025 observations with Bloomberg-derived estimates. On that basis, headline CPI is running at roughly 4.02% YoY in October, up from 3.74% in September.

The contribution breakdown is also notable:

• Core services: +2.06 percentage points
• Energy: +1.33 pp
• Food: +0.41 pp
• Core goods: +0.19 pp
That comes alongside the official October monthly readings of +0.4% headline and +0.3% core, both above consensus.

Methodology: Missing September 2025 weights are estimated by updating December 2024 weights for subsequent price changes, with the same weights used for October. Missing October 2025 index values are estimated as the geometric mean of September and November 2025.

These are Bloomberg-derived estimates, not official BLS figures.

Savoring life is taking a moment to smell the roses, enjoying a beautiful day, and making sure you have time with the people you love. Then there's the other side, which is accomplishment and impact.

You have to discover for yourself where you are and how you deal with those choices. The key, and the most effective path, is where they align—when you can make your work and your passion one and the same.

First, equity and the broader liquidity era as we know it is just so over. ZIRP is a thing of the past. 2026 has been an echo bubble. We are in a permanent high rates regime now. Capital is scarce

Second, in spite of this, I can't help feeling bullish digital assets. I have questioned my own stance on this multiple times, it seems like some sort of cognitive dissonance. But I think it one of the factors it comes down to is valuation

Digital assets where they are today, are, for the most part, extremely cheap compared to stocks and showing rapid growth. Now, people still want to make returns on capital. But the hurdle is far higher in these environments. As a result, you really only want to invest in strong companies.

Digital assets have a natural discount on the basis of having 1) supply come online every month, 2) lack of regulation and investor rights, and 3) no real future expectation of growth in an arena full of rugs, scams, and stage-left exits

If you were to ask me, gun to head, how I would allocate the portfolio of tomorrow, with no cash positions at all, optimizing purely for returns, i.e a portfolio with the most amount of torque and venture-like outcomes

it'd probably be something like:

33% digital-altcoins

33% AI-adjacent winners - software / robotics / bio / etc.

33% frontier tech - quantum / space / etc. 

That being said, these high risk assets are the first to go in these regimes. Sizing is key in these moments. Not too large at the beginning, yet not too small.

i've been testing gemini 4 carbon for 7 days. some early observations:

1/ it stopped cheating mostly. successful shortcuts on terminal-bench went to 0.0% (you can finally leave an agent alone mostly)

2/ prompt injection attack success rate was 0.0% on gray swan's benchmark. that's the number that lets you hand an agent your inbox

3/ it doesn't quit. google's own teams have watched it work on one problem for days and push through dead ends (love to see it)

4/ when it's stuck, it tells you what it still needs instead of making something up. unsupported claims got cut in half vs argon

5/ it does what you asked. not more, not less (overreach down 26%, under-delivering down 29%)

6/ it writes secure code at 2x the rate of argon. vibe coded apps keep getting hacked, so this one matters

7/ it found 88% of the vulnerabilities on sec-bench pro. every small company is about to have a security team it never hired

8/ $2 in and $10 out per million tokens to start, with cached input 95% off. agents that run for days just got cheap enough to actually run for days

9/ google shipped this two weeks after argon. pretty amazing pace

10/ cyber defenders got it first. very interesting

maybe i should do a full carbon vs fable 5.2 comparison on @startupideaspod.

🚨 HBM5 Doubles Bandwidth Without Adding a Single Pin 🚨

HBM5 keeps the same 2048 pins as HBM4E and runs each one nearly 2× faster. Samsung's Hot Chips 2026 presentation shows pin speed going from 14 Gbps on HBM4E to over 28 Gbps on HBM5.

Faster pins are only half the story. To keep each pin fed, everything behind the pins doubles too: DRAM banks, TSVs, and an upgraded PHY on the base die.
Here's how it works, explained as a grocery store 🛒 (1/6)🧵
